extracted.intended_audience: law and civic education project directors with little or no grant-writing experience
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for writing fundable grant proposals for law- and civic-education projects, aimed at new project directors; explains common proposal components, development steps before submission, and stewardship after funding. Emphasizes clarity, evidence of need, measurable objectives, realistic plans, evaluation, capacity, and budget justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduction/Summary/Abstract
rubrics_metrics.description: This section provides an opportunity to give a clear, concise, and well-organized overview of the proposal, using key words that the funding source has indicated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is usually where your project’s first impression is made and it should represent you in the best possible light. In brief form, according to the directions, tell who you are, what the needs you wish to address are, what you plan to do, how you will know when you have met your goals, and exactly what you want from the funding source. Federal and state proposal forms usually have a space for the abstract on the proposal cover sheet. Letters to foundations and corporations should begin with a summary addressing these points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statement of Needs (Stating the Problem)
rubrics_metrics.description: Clearly and concisely state the needs that the proposal is designed to address.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to statistics, research, demographics, national or state reports and studies showing that a problem exists, and documentation that the solution you propose may be effective. Briefly summarize research indicating promising practices in ameliorating the problem you describe. Carefully assess the needs you can reasonably address with your experience, your staff, and the funding you seek. Be careful not to delineate long term societal ills or vague concerns that you can not possibly have an impact on in a year or two, the duration of most grants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectives of the Proposal
rubrics_metrics.description: Objectives should describe the outcome if the agency agrees to fund your proposal and should be specific and measurable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objectives do not tell what you will do; they tell what will be the result of your funded activity. Explain specifically how these objectives meet the needs identified in the 'Statement of Needs' section above.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods / Activities / Plan of Action
rubrics_metrics.description: Specifically outline what you will do to meet each objective, including who will carry out each activity, oversight, and timeframe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate timelines and organizational charts if they are clear and useful. Estimate the number of people who will undertake each activity, and specify how they will be recruited. If you plan to seek out members of under-represented geographic areas or ethnic groups, specify how you plan to do so. Include hiring staff if required; meeting with advisory boards; preparing reports and evaluations; securing community involvement; involving families. If you plan to produce a product (e.g., lesson plans), describe approximate number of pages, format, method of production, and means of distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe your plan to appraise whether you have met the objectives outlined in your proposal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine how well you have carried out the funded activities and if those activities have met the needs described. Use evaluation to gather information necessary to plan and improve the project during the funded activity. Be sure the agency knows whether you plan to use subjective or objective evaluations and exactly what you hope to measure. Consider requesting funds to hire an evaluation specialist to design effective evaluation tools. Be specific about the type of evaluation you will provide at the end of the grant period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity of the Project / Qualifications of Staff
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrate why your agency and staff should be entrusted with funds and that you can carry out activities, fulfill objectives, and responsibly oversee the budget.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide information on the location and responsibilities of your agency; other supporters or cosponsors; how and when the project was started; record of success. If part of an institution, mention institutional commitment and services (e.g., accounting, office space). Include a brief summary of special qualifications of project director and other key personnel related to the objectives and activities to document likelihood of success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan for Continuation / Sustainability
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain how the project will be carried on after funding has ended and whether there is a reasonable expectation the project will continue without this funding source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Funders are greatly interested in institutionalization plans. Describe strategies to sustain services or institutionalize the developments created with the grant so the project does not depend indefinitely on the particular funding source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Budget and Budget Narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a budget narrative assuring the funder the budget is cost effective, reasonable, consistent with actual costs, and will enable you to carry out proposed activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show matching, in-kind, or other funding sources when possible. Follow the agency's directions on what they will and will not fund and the form they want you to use. Make sure everything you ask for in the budget is justified in the objectives and activities portion of your proposal.

rubrics_metrics.name: General Guidelines for Effective Proposals (Format, Style, Process)
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow directions precisely; organize information exactly as instructed; attend to scoring criteria and presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be attentive to how the proposal will be read and scored (point systems). Have a knowledgeable person read and score a draft before finalizing. The project director must read all drafts and examine the final product. Remove abbreviations, professional jargon, and assumptions that readers know internal references. Take care with appearance: professional document quality, correct pagination, spelling, and complete sentences are absolute requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attachments
rubrics_metrics.description: Include required or useful attachments as directed by the funder (assurances/certifications for federal/state grants).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow directions about whether attachments are acceptable, required, or not wanted. Consider including: list of influential/representative board members; edited resumes of key staff and consultants; map showing target areas; personally written letters from representative people who know your programs with specific language about past help and importance to children; agendas/newsletters/participant lists to document past successes; letter from key administrator assuring agency support (not complete funding); brief summary of research substantiating claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Before: Development Process (pre-submission cultivation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Activities to undertake before writing the full proposal to improve funding chances and eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contact agencies and organizations to learn funding interests and eligibility (often in person). Solicit program ideas from staff, constituents, board members, teachers, and students; talk to geographically and ethnically diverse stakeholders. Some agencies require preliminary proposals, concept papers, or position papers (3–5 pages) that include all components without detail and may lead to an invited proposal. Serve on committees and task forces that shape statewide goals and regulations. Invite key agency people to conferences and involve board/advisory members in outreach.

rubrics_metrics.name: After: Post-submission and Post-award Stewardship
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow-up actions after submission or award to maintain relationships, meet requirements, and improve future proposals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Send thank-you letters to helpers; keep funders informed about project progress and involve them in activities. Follow all reporting requirements and file complete information timely. Publicly recognize funders on program materials. Keep in touch with decision makers and agencies that have funded or not funded you; provide status reports or one- to two-page updates emphasizing funders' impact. Learn from successes and rejections: ask why you were not funded, read reviewers' scores and comments, and use feedback to improve future proposals. Persistence and daily fundraising effort are recommended.
